title: You're Just Not Enough, and Neither Am I
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart works through a paradox at the center of teaching: a teacher cannot force any student to master anything, yet remains the single most powerful influence on whether that student masters the subject this year. He traces the idea back to a workshop moment with colleagues in Indiana, where he told the room bluntly that none of them are good enough at their jobs to force mastery, framing this as liberating rather than defeatist. He extends the analogy to a physician, who cannot force a patient's cooperation yet still saves lives and changes their trajectory through skilled, realistic engagement with what is and isn't controllable. The essay's emotional turn is that accepting this limit, rather than denying it, is what allows a teacher to work from peace instead of anxiety, because care, while it can't be coerced, can be cultivated through sustained effort.
points: The core paradox Stuart names is that a teacher has zero power to force mastery but enormous power to influence whether it happens, and holding both truths at once is what he calls liberating rather than contradictory.
His physician analogy reframes lack of control as normal to skilled, high-stakes work rather than as a mark of failure, since doctors save lives without ever controlling patient cooperation.

The practical takeaway is that student care "can't be coerced" but "can absolutely be cultivated," which shifts the teacher's job from forcing compliance to deliberately building conditions for motivation.
quotes: I said, colleagues, you've got a problem. You are just not good enough at your job to force a student to master a single thing in your class. You just can't do it. And neither can I.

It reminds me a lot of what it must be like to be a general physician. You spend your whole life preparing for this job, you are constantly learning, constantly growing, constantly trying to be better.

And yet, without the cooperation of your patient, you're basically powerless. And then, even with the cooperation of your patient, there are so many things that you don't control. But nonetheless, great doctors save lives every year.
We must partner with the realities of our work. And one of those realities is that while care can't be coerced, you can't force a student to care about anything, care can absolutely be cultivated.
With that sense of both impotence and power comes a greater power that, apart from realism, I just don't think you can have.
You're just not enough to make your students care. But you absolutely, today in your work, will influence the degree to which they care.
